notes:
Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources I've gathered.

---

## Exodus 9 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview

This chapter covers three plagues — the fifth (murrain on livestock), the sixth (boils), and the seventh (hail) — and marks a turning point in the narrative: it is the first time the text explicitly says **the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart** (v. 12), and the first plague that threatens human life. Ellicott notes the plagues fall into triads; the seventh plague begins the third triad and introduces several new features: an unusually long warning (vv. 13–19), the first attack on human life on a large scale, unprecedented destruction to property and crops, and a test of Egyptian faith via a way of escape (vv. 20–21).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 1 — "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Go to Pharaoh and tell him that this is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let My people go, so that they may worship Me.'"

Gill notes this command came "the same day the plague of the flies was removed" and Moses is told to go "boldly, without any fear of him or his court." The demand — "Let My people go, that they may serve Me" — had been often made and, though reasonable, was refused.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

Guzik observes two things are clear in this appeal: (1) the people of Israel belonged to God, not to Pharaoh; (2) God wanted Pharaoh to release them for the LORD's own sake, not primarily for Israel's sake. This implies we should treat one another well "for the sake of the LORD" even more than for each other's sake.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-9/

Precept Austin notes this is "the freedom to worship formula" repeated about nine times across Exodus, and that Moses no longer shows any hesitation; he has grown in trust through each demonstration of God's sovereign power.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-9-commentary

---

### v. 2 — "But if you continue to restrain them and refuse to let them go…"

Gill simply says: "Continue to refuse, as he had done." The Pulpit Commentary notes that such repetitions are characteristic of ancient writings. The conditional warning is part of God's mercy — giving Pharaoh yet another opportunity to repent before judgment falls.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 3 — "…then the hand of the LORD will bring a severe plague on your livestock in the field — on your horses, donkeys, camels, herds, and flocks."

Ellicott identifies this as a "rinderpest, or murrain upon cattle" — a pestilence that unusually struck multiple domesticated species (horses, asses, camels, oxen, sheep). He notes horses were a comparatively recent import to Egypt (unknown before the Hyksos/Shepherd Dynasty) and were highly prized. Asses were the ordinary beasts of burden. Camels, though absent from Egyptian monuments, appear in inscriptions. The plague fell specifically on animals "in the field" — in the open air — since in Egypt a considerable portion of cattle was always housed.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

Gill calls it a "very grievous murrain" or "pestilence" — the Hebrew word often rendered "death" because pestilence sweeps away large numbers. The Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan render it simply "a death."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

The Pulpit Commentary observes that the plagues now shift from affecting persons (annoyance and pain) to affecting property.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 4 — "But the LORD will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, so that no animal belonging to the Israelites will die."

The Pulpit Commentary renders the Hebrew literally: "There shall not die of all that is the children's of Israel a thing." Gill notes the word used signifies "a marvellous separation" — even though the cattle of Israel breathed the same air, drank the same water, and fed in the same pastures, they were untouched. Ellicott observes that apparently Israel had been subjected to the first three plagues (which caused only annoyance), and their exemption began with the fourth plague and continued thereafter.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 5 — "The LORD set a time, saying, 'Tomorrow the LORD will do this in the land.'"

Ellicott explains that since murrain was not uncommon in Egypt (especially in the Delta), God marked its miraculous character by three things: (1) appointing an exact time, (2) exempting Israel's cattle, and (3) making it fatal to all Egyptian cattle left in the field. The delay ("tomorrow") also allowed any Egyptians who believed Moses to save their cattle by housing them.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

Gill concurs: God appointed a set time so "it might plainly appear it came from him, and was not owing to any natural cause."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 6 — "And the next day the LORD did just that. All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one animal belonging to the Israelites died."

Gill clarifies that "all" does not mean every single animal without exception, since livestock is mentioned later (v. 9, v. 19–21). Rather it means all that were in the field (v. 3), and "the greatest part of them, as Aben Ezra interprets it" — a limited sense in which "all" is frequently used in Scripture.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

Precept Austin emphasizes that the prophecy was perfectly fulfilled and the specific timing "substantiates it beyond a shadow of doubt as a miracle and not as some aberrational natural occurrence."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-9-commentary

Guzik notes this plague targeted the Egyptian goddess Hathor (a mother goddess in the form of a cow). Egyptian religion considered cattle sacred and the cow a symbol of fertility. He cites an ancient record where Egyptian soldiers refused to fire on advancing enemies because cattle had been placed in front of the opposing army.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-9/

---

### v. 7 — "Pharaoh sent officials and found that none of the livestock of the Israelites had died. But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not let the people go."

Gill observes that Pharaoh sent messengers to Goshen not just out of curiosity but perhaps hoping to find Israelite cattle dead so he could "confront" the prediction — or if they were alive, to seize them to make up his own losses. The Pulpit Commentary adds that Pharaoh may have attributed the Israelites' escape to their better care of cattle, better cattle-doctors, or the healthier air of Goshen. Ellicott notes the Hebrew word used here for "hardened" is *kābēd* — "heavy" or "dull." The king was less moved by loss of property than by previous plagues, since an absolute monarch could easily exact replacement value from his subjects.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 8 — "Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, 'Take handfuls of soot from the furnace; in the sight of Pharaoh, Moses is to toss it into the air.'"

The Pulpit Commentary says the object was "simply to show that as water, and earth and air could be turned into plagues, so fire could be." The "soot of the furnace" represented fire and was "peculiarly appropriate for the production of a disease which was in the main an 'inflammation.'" The act was done "toward heaven" to show the plague came from God, and "in the sight of Pharaoh" so he would be an eyewitness.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Gill notes the furnace may have been either a brick-kiln or a cooking furnace, since brick-kilns would scarcely be near Pharaoh's court. He suggests "perhaps some reference may be had to them, and to the labour of the children of Israel at them, and as a just retaliation for their oppression of them in that way."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

Ellicott similarly notes that much of Goshen had been converted into a brick-field (Exodus 1:14; 5:7–13), and "when ashes from one of these kilns were made the germs of a disease that was a sore infliction, their own wrongdoing became to the Egyptians a whip wherewith God scourged them."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 9 — "It will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and festering boils will break out on man and beast throughout the land."

The Pulpit Commentary renders the Hebrew literally: "an inflammation, begetting pustules." It says the description would apply to almost any eruptive disease and that attempts to determine exactly what the malady was "seem to be futile" since diseases change forms over millennia.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Precept Austin notes that this is part of the miracle — the soot "multiplies" and transforms from one substance (soot) into another (dust), and a small handful becomes enough to cover all Egypt. The dust then has "the miraculous power to produce boils and then sores."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-9-commentary

Gill describes "burning ulcers, hot carbuncles, rising up in pustules, blisters, and buboes, which last word is pretty near in sound with the Hebrew word here used."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

Guzik notes the Hebrew word for "boil" has the idea of "to burn" — a swelling, painful skin inflammation. This plague came without warning (as the third in its triad), and "for the first time the lives of humans are attacked and endangered, and thus it was a foreshadowing of the tenth and most dreadful of all the plagues" (citing Kaiser).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-9/

---

### v. 10 — "So they took soot from the furnace and stood before Pharaoh. Moses tossed it into the air, and festering boils broke out on man and beast."

The Pulpit Commentary notes the ordinary Hebrew word for furnace, *kibshon*, typically means "brick-kiln," though bricks were not often baked in Egypt. It suggests "either a brick-kiln or a furnace for the smelting of metals is meant."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Gill notes that this plague gave rise to "those lying scandalous stories of the Israelites being a scabby people, and of their being driven out of Egypt on that account, affirmed by Manetho, Lysimachus, Diodorus Siculus, Tacitus, Justin, and others."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 11 — "The magicians could not stand before Moses, because the boils had broken out on them and on all the Egyptians."

Ellicott observes it is uncertain whether the magicians were present accidentally or had come "for the express purpose of 'withstanding Moses' (2 Timothy 3:8)." He suspects the latter, "as the plague was made to fall with special violence upon them." The Pulpit Commentary says their persistency in attending despite previous failures was now punished: they were forced to quit the royal presence and hasten home to be nursed.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Guzik adds that this plague was probably directed against the Egyptian god Imhotep, said to be the god of medicine. "Even those who were thought to be closest to the Egyptian gods (the court magicians) were stricken."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-9/

---

### v. 12 — "But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said to Moses."

**This is a theologically significant verse — the first time the text says the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart.**

The Pulpit Commentary: "Up to this time the hardening of Pharaoh's heart has been ascribed to himself, or expressed indefinitely as a process that was continually going on — now for the first time it is positively stated that God hardened his heart, as he had threatened that he would (Exodus 4:21)."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Ellicott calls this "the judicial punitive hardening of Pharaoh's heart by God Himself." He compares it to Romans 1:28: "because they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind." The pattern: because Pharaoh had twice hardened himself — i.e., resisted an impression and crushed his inclination to yield (Exodus 8:15, 8:32) — God hardened him.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

Gill: "He having often, and so long hardened his own heart, God gave him up to judicial hardness of heart, to his own corruptions, the temptations of Satan, and the lying magicians about him."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic perspective): "Here, for the first time, it is said that the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh. Previously, God announced that he would harden Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 4:21, 7:3), and this was the fulfillment of it. Yet it is said at least six times before this that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exodus 7:13, 7:22, 8:15, 8:19, 8:32, 9:7). We see that God's hardening of Pharaoh's heart was the strengthening of what he already had set himself towards." He quotes Cole: "The moral would be that God hardens those who harden themselves," and Thomas: "'Harden' is the expression, not of the divine purpose but of the result of disobedience to the divine appeals."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-9/

**Denominational differences on this verse:** Though I could not retrieve separate pages from each tradition's sites, the hardened-heart theme is a classic dividing line. The Reformed tradition (e.g., Calvin, and later Ligonier, Desiring God) typically stresses divine sovereignty in hardening as part of God's decree — using Romans 9:17–18 to teach unconditional election. The Wesleyan/Methodist and Pentecostal traditions (as reflected in Guzik/Enduring Word) tend to emphasise that God's hardening is judicial — a response to prior human free choice — preserving genuine human responsibility alongside divine sovereignty. Gill (a Baptist of the Reformed/Calvinistic variety) presents it as "judicial hardness." Ellicott (Anglican) likewise calls it "judicial punitive hardening."

---

### v. 13 — "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Get up early in the morning, stand before Pharaoh, and tell him that this is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let My people go, so that they may worship Me.'"

The Pulpit Commentary notes the practice of Egyptian kings rising early to dispatch business (recorded by Herodotus), and that the identical message is repeated "as a token of God's unchangingness."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 14 — "Otherwise, I will send all My plagues against you and your officials and your people, so you may know that there is no one like Me in all the earth."

The Pulpit Commentary calls this "a very emphatic announcement." "At this time" contrasts the immediate future with the past: "the hour of mild warnings and slight plagues is gone by. Now he is to expect something far more terrible." The phrase "send all my plagues upon thine heart" (KJV) means each plague "will strike a blow on that perverse and obdurate heart — each will stir his nature to its inmost depths."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Gill explains "all my plagues" does not mean every plague in God's power, but "all that he had determined in his mind to bring upon him." These plagues would reach Pharaoh's heart, filling him "with horror and terror," not merely affecting his body as the boils had.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

Ellicott adds the purpose clause: the naturally obdurate heart, further hardened by Pharaoh's own voluntary action (8:15, 8:32) and now hardened penally by God (9:12), "was now to be softened by a repetition of blow after blow, until it should finally succumb."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 15 — "For by this time I could have stretched out My hand and struck you and your people with a plague to wipe you off the earth."

Both Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary agree the standard English translation "I will stretch out my hand" is mistaken. The correct sense is past/conditional: "And now I might have stretched out mine hand, and smitten both thee and thy people with pestilence; and then thou hadst been cut off from the earth" (Ellicott). The point: God is saying "I could have destroyed you already, but I have not. Why? See the next verse."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Gill likewise: "For when now I stretched out my hand, or if now I had stretched out my hand to smite thee and thy people with pestilence" — at the time of the cattle murrain, God could have smitten the people too.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 16 — "But I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power to you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth."

**This is one of the most theologically significant verses in Exodus, quoted by Paul in Romans 9:17.**

Ellicott translates: "But truly on this account have I made thee stand — i.e., kept thee alive, not for thy deserts, not even in pity, but only 'for to show in thee My power.' Thou hast provoked Me so that long since thou wouldst have been 'cut off from the earth,' only that My glory will be the more shown forth by thy continuance in life."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

The Pulpit Commentary similarly: "But truly for this cause have I caused thee to stand," i.e., "kept thee alive and sustained thee in the position thou occupiest… to impress thee, if it is possible that thou canst be impressed, with the greatness of my power… and also that my name may be declared throughout all the earth — i.e., that attention may be called widely among the neighbouring nations to the great truth that there is really but one God."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Gill: "Instead of smiting thee with the pestilence, and cutting thee off… 'I have raised thee up'; made thee to stand, to continue in being; I have preserved thine from perishing by the former plagues, and have reserved thee for greater judgments and sorer punishments."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

Guzik: "If Pharaoh thought he was accomplishing anything with his resistance against God, he was completely wrong. All his stubborn rebellion merely glorified the LORD more in the end."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-9/

**Denominational difference:** In the Reformed tradition (e.g., Calvin, Jonathan Edwards, John Piper at desiringgod.org), Romans 9:17 citing this verse is foundational for the doctrine of unconditional election and double predestination — God "raised up" Pharaoh specifically to display His power in destroying him. The Wesleyan/Arminian tradition reads "raised you up" as God bringing Pharaoh to the throne providentially, foreknowing his rebellion, and using his freely chosen evil for a greater good. The Pentecostal reading (Guzik) tends toward the latter, emphasising Pharaoh's own responsibility. Unfortunately, I was unable to retrieve separate pages from ligonier.org, desiringgod.org, or seedbed.com for direct quotations on this verse.

---

### v. 17 — "Still, you lord it over My people and do not allow them to go."

The Cambridge Bible notes the Hebrew verb is unique, found only here: the root means "to cast up a way" (Isaiah 57:14, 62:10), related to words for "siege-mound" and "highway." Hence the sense: "raisest thyself up as a mound (or obstacle) against my people."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/exodus/9.htm

The Pulpit Commentary renders: "Dost thou still oppose thyself against my people, so as not to let them go." The verb translated "exalt" in the KJV is strictly "to raise a mound, or bank," thence "to obstruct, oppose."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Gill: "Dost thou still tread upon my people? trample them under foot, and make an highway or causeway of them."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 18 — "Behold, at this time tomorrow I will rain down the worst hail that has ever fallen on Egypt, from the day it was founded until now."

The Pulpit Commentary notes that "a more exact note of time than usual was here given" (compare 8:23; 9:5). Rain and hail are relatively rare in Egypt, though not as rare as some ancient authors claimed. A storm like this one would be "quite strange and abnormal; no Egyptian would have experienced anything approaching to it."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Ellicott confirms: thunderstorms are especially uncommon in Egypt and when they occur are for the most part mild. The expression "since the foundation thereof" means "since Egypt became a nation" (not since the creation of the physical land).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 19 — "So give orders now to shelter your livestock and everything you have in the field. Every man or beast that remains in the field and is not brought inside will die when the hail comes down upon them."

Ellicott explains that "the peculiar circumstances of Egypt, where the whole country was overflowed by the Nile during some months of each year, caused the provision of shelter for cattle to be abnormally great." During inundation season, all cattle had to be gathered into sheds and cattle-yards. Thus it would have been "easy to house all the cattle that remained to the Egyptians after the murrain, if the warning here given had been attended to generally."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

Guzik highlights God's mercy: "God invited Pharaoh and the Egyptians to trust Him by recommending precautions before the plague." He cites Kaiser: "Rainfall comes so occasionally in Upper Egypt that the prediction of a severe hailstorm accompanied by a violent electrical storm must have been greeted with much skepticism."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-9/

The Pulpit Commentary notes that **human life was now for the first time threatened**: herdsmen who remained in the open field would be killed by the huge hailstones.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

---

### vv. 20–21 — "Those among Pharaoh's officials who feared the word of the LORD hurried… but those who disregarded the word of the LORD left their servants and livestock in the field."

The Pulpit Commentary calls it "a new fact that any of the Egyptians had been brought to 'fear the word of Jehovah.'" Probably the effect of the plagues had been "gradually to convince a considerable number, not so much that Jehovah was the one True God as that he was a great and powerful god, whose chastisements were to be feared."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Ellicott compares this to the response to the Gospel: "Some believed the things which were spoken, and some believed not" (Acts 28:24).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

Gill notes: "He that feared the word of the Lord… made his servants and cattle flee into the houses… in which he acted the wise and prudent part." The one who disregarded it "set not his heart unto it, took no notice of it, but treated it with the utmost contempt."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 22 — "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that hail may fall on all the land of Egypt — on man and beast and every plant of the field throughout the land of Egypt.'"

The Pulpit Commentary notes the act is appropriate, "as the plague was to come from the heaven." Similarly, in earlier plagues, Aaron's hand was stretched upon the waters (first and second plagues) and upon the dust (third plague).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Gill observes the hail would cover "all the land of Egypt" — unusual for a hailstorm, which "seldom reaches far, a mile it may be, or some such space; but never was such an one heard of as to reach through a whole country."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 23 — "So Moses stretched out his staff toward heaven, and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and lightning struck the earth. So the LORD rained down hail upon the land of Egypt."

Ellicott translates the Hebrew for "the fire ran along upon the ground" more literally as "fire walked earthwards." He notes that some (Aben-Ezra, Canon Cook) think the phenomenon was not ordinary lightning but something akin to "fire-balls" — where the electric fluid has "something of permanency, continuing several seconds, or even minutes."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

The Pulpit Commentary says: "Some very peculiar electrical display seems to be intended — something corresponding to the phenomena called 'fireballs,' where the electric fluid does not merely flash momentarily, but remains for several seconds, or even minutes, before it disappears."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Gill notes that Artapanus, a heathen writer, records this storm saying "Moses, besides the hail, caused earthquakes by night."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 24 — "The hail fell and the lightning continued flashing through it. The hail was so severe that nothing like it had ever been seen in all the land of Egypt from the time it became a nation."

The Pulpit Commentary renders: "There was hail, and in the midst of the hail a fire infolding itself" — the same expression used in Ezekiel 1:4. "It seems to mean a fire that was not a mere flash, but collected itself into a mass and was seen for some considerable time."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Guzik quotes Trapp: "A strange mixture; a miracle within a miracle, saith Rabbi Solomon. Fire and water made a peace betwixt themselves, that they might obey the will of their Creator."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-9/

---

### v. 25 — "Throughout the land of Egypt, the hail struck down everything in the field, both man and beast; it beat down every plant of the field and stripped every tree."

The Pulpit Commentary clarifies it was the hail — not the lightning — that is attributed with the great destruction. It notes that even in temperate climates, hailstorms occasionally do such severe crop damage that "it has been found desirable to organise a special insurance against loss from this cause." The trees were not broken to fragments but the "smaller branches and twigs" were broken off, destroying the prospect of fruit.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 26 — "The only place where it did not hail was in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived."

All commentators note the continuation of the pattern of distinction. This is the third explicit mention of Goshen's exemption (cf. 8:22; 9:4).

---

### v. 27 — "Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron. 'This time I have sinned,' he said. 'The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked.'"

The Pulpit Commentary: "I acknowledge this time that I have sinned… I do not any longer maintain that my conduct has been right." The confession was extorted by the terrible, continuing nature of the storm. However, it notes "there is perhaps some shifting of sin, that was all his own, upon the Egyptian 'people,' which indicates disingenuousness." The literal Hebrew: "Jehovah is the Just One; and I and my people are the sinners."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Guzik: "This sounds like perfect words of repentance from Pharaoh, but true repentance had not worked its way into his heart. Pharaoh was grieved at the consequences of sin, but not at the sin itself." He notes that Pharaoh's "I have sinned" is one of eight such confessions in Scripture, and it is insincere — comparable to Balaam (Numbers 22:34), Achan (Joshua 7:20), Saul (1 Samuel 15:24), and Judas (Matthew 27:4).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-9/

---

### v. 28 — "Pray to the LORD, for there has been enough of God's thunder and hail. I will let you go; you do not need to stay any longer."

The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew "mighty thunderings" is literally "voices of God" — thunder was regarded by many ancient nations as the actual voice of a god. In the Vedic theology, Indra spoke in thunder.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 29 — "Moses said to him, 'When I have left the city, I will spread out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth is the LORD's.'"

The Pulpit Commentary explains that Moses and Aaron apparently did not live in the city (Tanis/Zoan) but in the country with the other Israelites. Moses undertakes to pray "as soon as I am outside the city walls." The phrase "that the earth is the LORD's" may mean either "the whole earth is Jehovah's" or "the land (of Egypt) is His." This plague — coming from the open heaven that surrounds the whole world — indicated that the entire earth was His, not just Egypt.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Ellicott: "It was the general belief of the Egyptians, as of most ancient nations, that each country had its own god or gods. Pharaoh had already admitted Jehovah's power (Exodus 8:8), and now regarded Him as the God of the Hebrews (Exodus 8:28). God desired to have it generally acknowledged that He was the God of the whole earth."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 30 — "But as for you and your officials, I know that you still do not fear the LORD our God."

The Pulpit Commentary: "True fear of God is shown by obedience to his commands. Pharaoh and his servants had the sort of fear which devils have — 'they believed and trembled.' But they had not yet that real reverential fear which is joined with love, and has, as its fruit, obedience."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Guzik observes: "Moses' response to Pharaoh showed that he was starting to learn and to discern. Moses knew the promise to touch Pharaoh's firstborn had not yet been fulfilled (Exodus 4:22–23)."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-9/

Gill: "Notwithstanding the confession of sin he had made… I know that ye will not yet fear the Lord God: they had not feared him yet; the confession of sin made did not arise from the true fear of God, but from a dread of punishment."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 31 — "(Now the flax and barley were destroyed, since the barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom…)"

The Pulpit Commentary says these verses "seem out of place, containing, as they do, an account of the damage done by the hail, and being thus exegetical of Exodus 9:25. They are a sort of afterthought, inserted parenthetically, and prepare the way for the understanding of the next plague; since, if the damage done by the hail had extended to all the crops, there would have been nothing left for the locusts to devour."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Ellicott provides agricultural detail: Flax was grown largely in Egypt because linen garments were universally worn and were the necessary attire of priests; mummies were swathed in linen bandages. Barley was grown as horse food, for beer, and for an inferior kind of bread. The flax forms its seed-vessel toward the end of January or beginning of February, and the barley comes into ear about the same time. These facts **fix the date of this plague** and help date both earlier and later ones.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 32 — "…but the wheat and spelt were not destroyed, because they are late crops."

Ellicott notes "rie" (KJV) is a wrong translation — rye has never been grown in Egypt. The Hebrew *cussemeth* refers to the *holcus sorghum* (doora), the only grain besides wheat and barley represented on Egyptian monuments. Wheat is a full month later than barley, coming into ear in March. The holcus sorghum, if sown with wheat, would ripen about the same period.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

The Pulpit Commentary confirms rye "was not grown in Egypt" and the word means doora.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 33 — "Then Moses departed from Pharaoh, went out of the city, and spread out his hands to the LORD. The thunder and hail ceased, and the rain no longer poured down on the land."

The Pulpit Commentary notes that rain "had not been previously mentioned, as it was no part of the plague, that is, it caused no damage. But Moses, recording the cessation as an eye-witness, recollects that rain was mingled with the hail, and that, at his prayer, the thunder, the hail, and the rain all ceased. The touch is one which no later writer would have introduced."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Ellicott: "Moses did not fear the storm. Though it still raged, he quitted the shelter of the city, and went out into the midst of it, and spread out his hands to God, when lo! at once the rain, and hail, and thunder ceased at his bidding." He quotes Millington: "Moses knew that he was safe, though all around might be destroyed; the very hairs of his head were all numbered, not one of them could perish."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

---

### v. 34 — "When Pharaoh saw that the rain and hail and thunder had ceased, he sinned again and hardened his heart — he and his officials."

Ellicott: "As Pharaoh had never been so much moved previously, so it now required a greater effort of his will to 'harden his heart' than it had ever done before; and thus he now 'sinned yet more' than he had as yet sinned. It seems strange that the mercy of God should still have allowed him one other chance (Exodus 10:3–6)."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-9.html

The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew verb here is *kabad* (the weakest of the three hardening verbs — meaning "to be dull" or "heavy"), distinct from *qashah* ("to be hard") and *khazaq* ("fixed and stubborn resolution"). Pharaoh's "servants" — the officers of his court — still upheld him at this point, though their tone would change after the eighth plague (Exodus 10:7).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-9.html

Guzik: "Hardening the heart against God is sin; failing to repent when God graciously answers our plea and ignoring His rich mercy is to sin yet more."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-9/

---

### v. 35 — "So Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not let the Israelites go, just as the LORD had said through Moses."

The threefold pattern concludes: Pharaoh's heart, hardened, matches exactly what God had foretold. Guzik closes: "All went according to God's plan, even the hardness of Pharaoh's heart."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-9/

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

**On the hardening of Pharaoh's heart (vv. 7, 12, 34–35):** All the commentaries consulted agree on a common traditional reading: Pharaoh first hardened his own heart (six times mentioned before v. 12), and only then did God judicially harden him. Gill (Reformed Baptist) frames it as "judicial hardness." Ellicott (Anglican) calls it "judicial punitive hardening." Guzik (charismatic/evangelical) emphasises it as "the strengthening of what he already had set himself towards." The difference between Reformed/Calvinistic and Arminian/Wesleyan readings lies in whether God's hardening is seen primarily as an outworking of His eternal decree (Reformed) or as a judicial response to prior human free choice (Arminian/Wesleyan/Pentecostal). The sites needed to quote each tradition directly on this passage were not retrievable within the search limit.

**On v. 16 ("raised you up"):** This is the classic Romans 9:17 proof-text for the Reformed doctrine of God's sovereignty in election. The Reformed reading sees God as actively raising Pharaoh up for the purpose of displaying wrath. The alternative reading (reflected in Guzik and the older commentaries) stresses that God "kept Pharaoh standing" (preserved him) rather than orchestrating his rebellion — using his freely chosen evil for a greater good.

**On the plague of hail (vv. 18–26):** Unanimous among the commentators that this was miraculous: hail of unprecedented severity in a land where rain and hail are rare, fire intermingled with hail, and a precise prediction of timing. The parenthetical agricultural note (vv. 31–32) is considered by the Pulpit Commentary as an authentic eyewitness touch that also prepares the narrative for the locust plague.

**On Pharaoh's false repentance (vv. 27–35):** Consistent across traditions: Pharaoh's confession is paradigmatic of false repentance — sorrow over consequences rather than godly sorrow over sin. Moses' discernment in v. 30 ("I know that you still do not fear the LORD") shows spiritual maturity.
